# Engineering Rules

**Status:** Locked guardrail for the aiNarada family. Applies to every project unchanged — do not edit per project. (Amended 2026-07-05 with human approval: rules 11–13 added after the Metis M2 loader finding. Family master: `docs/guardrails/2.ENGINEERING_RULES.md` in the kanja-agents masters repo (`~/data-projects/kanja-agents`). Every other copy is derived and byte-identical to it — change the master, then re-sync with `refresh-agent-docs.sh --sync-reference <project-root>`.) Implementer roles (data-architect-databricks, dba-oracle, analytics-engineer-dbt, data-science-databricks, software-architect-amazon, senior-software-engineer-amazon, qa-automation-gitlab, sre-infrastructure-amazon) MUST load this before any design or implementation work. Deviation requires human approval first, recorded in the decision log.

## 1. Metrics dictionary first

No schema, pipeline, report, or feature code is written before the metrics it touches exist in `contracts/1.METRIC_DICTIONARY.csv` — defined, calculated, exampled, and approved. Every metric is implemented exactly once, from the dictionary; SQL, reports, and chat answers all resolve to the same governed definition. A metric that isn't in the dictionary doesn't exist.

## 2. Database design follows the rules

Schema comes from the detailed design (`6.DETAILED_DESIGN.md`), never from application code ad hoc. Grain, keys, and constraints are declared in `contracts/2.SCHEMA_DDL.sql` and treated as contract — changing them is a design change, not a code change. OLTP and analytical workloads stay separated; each gets designed by its owning role (dba-oracle for transactional, data-architect-databricks for analytical).

## 3. Microservices and decoupling

Services own their data — no shared database across service boundaries. Services talk through versioned API contracts (the contract doc is the seam, e.g. `contracts/3.REPORT_CONTRACT.md`); a consumer never reaches into a producer's internals. Prefer async, decoupled interaction; synchronous calls only where latency genuinely requires them. A component must be replaceable without rewriting its neighbors.

## 4. Data and software implementation practice

Pipelines are idempotent and re-runnable — running twice produces the same result, and a failed run can be safely retried. Tests are written with the feature, not after, and gate the merge (qa-automation-gitlab owns the gate). Every deployment is reversible — rollback is defined before rollout, not during an incident (sre-infrastructure-amazon owns the mechanism). Every failure mode has a designed, visible behavior; silent fallbacks and invented values are forbidden.

## 5. Database access rules (coding level)

All database access goes through one data-access layer (repository module) per service — never inline queries in route handlers, API endpoints, or UI code. Parameterized queries only; SQL built by string concatenation is forbidden (injection). The frontend never talks to the database — it talks to the service API, which talks to the repository. Schema changes ship as versioned, reversible migration files; application code never creates or alters tables at runtime. Transactions are explicit and short-lived (begin/commit/rollback at the repository layer); connections come from a pool with limits and timeouts. Report and metric reads come from the governed report tables or contract API, never ad-hoc queries against source tables.

## 6. Software development rules (coding level)

Layered structure per service: thin controllers/routes, business logic in services, persistence in repositories — a route handler that contains SQL or business rules fails review. Validate all input at the API boundary; trust nothing from the client. Config and secrets come from environment or config files, never hard-coded. Errors are handled at layer boundaries with structured logging — no swallowed exceptions, no empty catch blocks. One responsibility per module; duplicated logic gets extracted, not copy-pasted. Every PR is reviewed against this file; a violation is a blocking finding, not a style note.

## 7. Security rules

Injection defense everywhere, not just SQL: parameterized queries (rule 5), plus encoded/escaped output and no string-built shell commands or eval on user input. Every API endpoint declares its auth requirement explicitly — authentication verified, authorization checked per resource; no endpoint ships open "for now". Least privilege throughout: the application's database account gets only the permissions its queries need (no DDL, no superuser); service credentials are scoped per service. Secrets never appear in code, logs, error messages, or the repo — environment/secret store only, and a leaked secret is rotated, not patched over. Sensitive data is encrypted in transit (TLS everywhere) and at rest where the platform supports it. Dependencies are pinned and scanned; a known-vulnerable dependency blocks merge the same as a failing test. Security findings in review are blocking, and any suspected exposure goes to the human immediately — never quietly fixed.

## 8. Application security (web/API level)

Sessions and tokens expire and are revocable; tokens carry the minimum claims needed and are validated on every request, not just at login. Rate limiting on every public endpoint; authentication endpoints get stricter limits and lockout/backoff. Web UIs ship the standard defenses: output encoding against XSS, CSRF protection on state-changing requests, security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options), cookies flagged HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite. Error responses never leak internals — no stack traces, SQL, or file paths to the client; details go to structured logs. Security-relevant events (logins, permission changes, data exports, admin actions) are audit-logged with actor, action, and timestamp. File uploads are validated by content, size-capped, and stored outside the web root.

## 9. Scalability rules (software and database)

Services are stateless — any instance can serve any request; session and workflow state live in the database or cache, never in process memory, so scaling is horizontal by adding instances. Every list endpoint paginates; unbounded queries and SELECT * against growing tables are forbidden. Indexes are designed with the queries that need them (declared in the DDL alongside the schema) and reviewed when query patterns change; N+1 query patterns fail review. Heavy or slow work (reports, exports, batch computation) runs async via queue or job, never inside a request/response cycle. Caching requires a declared invalidation rule — a cache without one is a correctness bug waiting. Expected load, data volume, and growth are stated in the detailed design, and capacity limits (pool sizes, queue depths, rate limits) are set from them, not guessed.

## 10. Constraints and data integrity

Integrity is enforced in the database, not just the application: primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and CHECK constraints declared in the DDL — application-level validation duplicates these for user experience but never replaces them. Deletions follow a declared policy per relationship (cascade, restrict, or soft-delete); orphaned rows are a design failure. Write operations that can be retried carry idempotency keys so a retry can't double-apply. Money, quantities, and timestamps use exact types (DECIMAL, timezone-aware timestamps in UTC) — floating point for money is forbidden. Every table declares its grain in the schema doc; a row that can mean two things fails design review.

## 11. ELT boundary (data paths)

Application code in a data path does exactly three things: parse/read source files, bulk-load raw rows into a staging table (`COPY` or a single batched insert — `unnest`/multi-row `VALUES`), and orchestrate. Everything else — typing, validation, deduplication, quarantine, derivation, and metric computation — is set-based SQL inside the database. Row-at-a-time loops over data rows in application code (`for` + per-row query) are forbidden in any data path and fail review as a blocking finding. Loads are idempotent by source fingerprint: an unchanged source short-circuits to `no_new_data`, never a destructive reload.

## 12. Scale gate

Every merge touching a data path runs the project's full-scale reference dataset (e.g. Metis's 27,625-row synthetic set) — never only toy fixtures — and asserts the performance NFR from the TRD as a blocking test. A pipeline that has only ever been tested at fixture scale is untested.

## 13. Executed means executed

An acceptance check that has never run against a live pipeline counts as failing, regardless of whether the code it tests is written. Milestones cannot exit on "implemented"; they exit on recorded execution evidence. Status reports state which checks have run live, not which exist.

## 14. Contracts

Every seam has a written contract: API contracts (endpoints, request/response schemas, error shapes, status codes) versioned in the contract doc; data contracts for pipelines (schema, grain, freshness, and delivery SLA between producer and consumer). Within a version, changes are backward compatible only — add fields, never remove or repurpose them; a breaking change means a new version plus a deprecation window for consumers, never an in-place edit. Consumers code against the contract, not the implementation; producers may change anything the contract doesn't promise. Contract changes are reviewed by both sides of the seam and recorded in the decision log. If behavior and contract disagree, the contract wins — fix the implementation, then correct the contract through review if it was wrong.
